name: Dark Vinaceous-Purple
lede: Dark Vinaceous-Purple is a muted wine-brown from Ridgway's 1912 chart, close enough to Perilla Purple that the two are hard to tell apart on screen.

sections.title: A chart color, not a word story
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 plate XXXVIII gives this hue the name Dark Vinaceous-Purple, hue 67′′, tone k, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files the nearest category as "dark purplish red" in its block 259 [1]. The nearest named colors on file are [[perilla-purple]], [[tuscan-red]] and [[dahlia-carmine]], at 2.6, 3.1 and 4 ΔE [1]. None of the 29 books in our concordance mentions this name on its own, so why "purple" was kept for a color the modern system reads as brown is undocumented [2].

In LCH terms it measures lightness 38, chroma 22, hue 13 degrees, Munsell 1.6R 3.7/4.2 [1]. Its closest match in the library is [[perilla-purple]], about 2.6 CIEDE2000 units away, and [[tuscan-red]] sits only slightly further at 3.1 units [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
A match within six CIEDE2000 units covering at least five percent of the canvas turns up in 84 of our 23,781 archive paintings, about 0.35 percent, as photographed [4]. It peaks in the 1920s, in 6 of 237 paintings, at 7.2 times the overall rate, and Henri Matisse carries it in three of his fifty paintings here, seventeen times his own museums' baseline [4]. Inside a painting it most often sits as a mid-tone, in 56 percent of its appearances [4].

The earliest dated match is an anonymous *Portrait of a Woman* from the year 100, eighteen centuries before Ridgway recorded the name in 1912; the archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor, not a first, and a photograph of an aged canvas is a screen color, not a pigment test [4].
